summary: Describes the Cryptographic Message Syntax, a format for digitally signing, digesting, authenticating or encrypting arbitrary message content. It is a building block used by S/MIME and many other security systems. It was replaced by RFC 5652.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a standard kind of envelope for protecting messages with locks and signatures. It was replaced by RFC 5652.

questions: what is enveloped data in cms
subtitle: A general envelope format for signing, hashing, authenticating or encrypting any message content.

tldr.problem: Many protocols need to sign or encrypt arbitrary data and carry the result in a standard form, including more than one layer of protection on the same content.
tldr.mechanism: CMS defines an ASN.1 wrapper called ContentInfo that holds one of six content types (data, signed-data, enveloped-data, digested-data, encrypted-data, authenticated-data), which can be nested inside one another.
tldr.outcome: CMS grew out of PKCS #7 version 1.5 and is used by several IETF standards-track protocols. RFC 3852 was obsoleted by RFC 5652 and was updated by RFC 4853 and RFC 5083.

today: RFC 3852 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 5652, so new work should read that RFC. It was itself the replacement for RFC 3369 and was updated by RFC 4853 and RFC 5083.

sections.title: What CMS Is and Where It Came From
sections.content:
The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) is a syntax used to digitally sign, digest, authenticate or encrypt arbitrary message content. It is an encapsulation syntax: one envelope can be nested inside another, and one party can sign data that was already encapsulated. Attributes such as signing time can be signed along with the content, and others, such as countersignatures, can be attached to a signature.

CMS values are described in ASN.1 and encoded with BER. The RFC notes that many electronic mail systems cannot carry arbitrary octet strings reliably, and it does not define any encoding for that case.

CMS is derived from PKCS #7 version 1.5 (RFC 2315), which was first published by RSA Laboratories in November 1993. RFC 2630 was the first CMS version on the IETF standards track, and RFC 3369 added password-based key management and an extension mechanism for new key management schemes. This document obsoletes RFC 3369, adds a similar extension mechanism for new certificate and revocation formats, fixes errata and clarifies the countersignature text. Specific cryptographic algorithms were moved to a separate document, and CMS itself does not require any particular algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: CMS is a grown-up version of an older way of putting a message in a locked, signed envelope. Over the years the rules were improved so the envelope could hold new kinds of locks.

sections.title: The ContentInfo Wrapper and Six Content Types
sections.content:
Everything in CMS is carried in ContentInfo, which holds a contentType (an object identifier) and the content itself. This document defines six content types: data, signed-data, enveloped-data, digested-data, encrypted-data and authenticated-data. Others can be defined outside the document.

An implementation MUST implement ContentInfo and MUST implement the data, signed-data and enveloped-data types. The other three MAY be implemented. The data type is just arbitrary octet strings, with interpretation left to the application, and it is generally wrapped inside one of the other types. S/MIME uses it to identify MIME-encoded content.

As a design goal, each type allows single-pass processing using indefinite-length BER, which helps with large content or content piped from another process. The drawback is that DER is hard to produce in one pass. Signed attributes and authenticated attributes are the only data CMS requires in DER, so recipients can verify content that has attributes they do not recognise.

Each major structure starts with a version number. The lowest version number that supports the syntax actually used is the one to send, to maximize interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one outer envelope, and it says what kind of thing is inside. There are six kinds, such as signed, locked, or just a fingerprint.

sections.title: Signed-data
sections.content:
Signed-data holds content of any type and zero or more signatures, so any number of signers can sign in parallel. To build it, each signer computes a message digest (hash) of the content, signs that digest with a private key, and puts the signature and signer details in a SignerInfo. Certificates and CRLs are gathered in, and everything is collected with the content into a SignedData value.

A recipient recomputes the digest and uses the signer's public key to verify the signature. The key is found through the issuer name and serial number, or through a subject key identifier, and the signer's certificate MAY be included in the message. The recipient MUST NOT rely on digest values computed by the originator.

If signedAttrs is present, it MUST be DER encoded and MUST contain at least a content-type attribute and a message-digest attribute; it MUST be present when the content type is not id-data. In that case the digest that is signed covers the attributes, which in turn carry the content digest. The content itself may be omitted from the message to make an "external signature".

The RFC warns about subtle incompatibilities with PKCS #7 when the content is not the plain Data type, and describes a fallback decoding strategy.
sections.plainLanguage: Signed-data is a letter plus a stamp that only you can make. Anyone can check the stamp matches the letter, and several people can add their own stamps.

sections.title: Enveloped-data and Key Management
sections.content:
Enveloped-data carries encrypted content plus a way for each recipient to recover the key. The sender generates a random content-encryption key, encrypts the content with it, then encrypts that key separately for each recipient. The same content-encryption algorithm and key are used for all recipients, and there MUST be at least one recipient.

Four techniques are supported for protecting the key, each with its own RecipientInfo alternative:

  • Key transport (ktri): the key is encrypted in the recipient's public key.
  • Key agreement (kari): the sender's private key and the recipient's public key make a pairwise key that encrypts the content-encryption key.
  • Previously distributed symmetric keys (kekri): a shared key-encryption key is used.
  • Passwords (pwri): the key-encryption key is derived from a password or shared secret.

Implementations MUST support ktri, kari and kekri, and MAY support pwri. A further ori alternative lets future documents define other key management techniques, and unknown alternatives MUST be handled gracefully. Where an algorithm needs input padded to a multiple of k octets (k less than 256), the padding bytes each carry the value of the padding length.
sections.plainLanguage: You lock the message with one random key, then make a copy of that key for each friend, each locked in a way only that friend can open.

sections.title: Digested, Encrypted and Authenticated Data
sections.content:
Digested-data holds content and a message digest of it. It is typically used for integrity, and the result usually becomes input to enveloped-data. Its version is 0 if the content type is id-data and 2 otherwise.

Encrypted-data is encrypted content with no recipients and no encrypted keys, so keys MUST be managed by other means. The RFC gives local storage, perhaps with a key derived from a password, as the typical use.

Authenticated-data carries content, a message authentication code (MAC), and recipient information that conveys the MAC key. The MAC covers the content directly, or the DER encoding of the authenticated attributes if they are present; with attributes, a content-type and a message-digest attribute MUST be included. The recipient MUST NOT rely on MAC or digest values computed by the originator, and authentication succeeds only if the recipient's computed MAC equals the mac field.

Several shared helper types complete the picture. Algorithm identifiers all use the X.509 AlgorithmIdentifier type. Certificates may be X.509 certificates or other formats, and revocation information is usually a CRL, with an other alternative that can carry formats such as OCSP responses. The older PKCS #6 certificates and version 1 attribute certificates are obsolete and SHOULD NOT be used.
sections.plainLanguage: Digested is a fingerprint of the message. Encrypted is a locked box where you already share the key. Authenticated is a seal that proves the message was not changed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists what implementers must protect: the signer's private key (compromise permits masquerade), and the key management private key, key-encryption key and content-encryption key (compromise may disclose protected content). Compromise of the message-authentication key may allow undetectable modification.

The key management technique used to distribute message-authentication keys must itself provide data origin authentication. RSA and Ephemeral-Static Diffie-Hellman do not, while Static-Static Diffie-Hellman does when both public keys are bound to identities in X.509 certificates. When more than two parties share a MAC key, the content could come from any of them.

Keys, IVs and padding must be randomly generated, and weak pseudo-random generators can leave little or no security. If the key-encryption and content-encryption algorithms differ, the effective security is that of the weaker one: the RFC's example is a 168-bit Triple-DES key wrapped with a 40-bit RC2 key, which gives at most 40 bits of protection. Algorithm implementations should be modular because algorithms weaken over time.

Countersignatures sign only the signature value, so implementations should verify the original signature first or countersign only in a context that guarantees an appropriate value.
sections.plainLanguage: Guard your keys, make them from truly random numbers, and remember a chain is only as strong as its weakest link.

items.title: data
items.text: Arbitrary octet strings; meaning is left to the application.

items.title: signed-data
items.text: Content plus zero or more signatures.

items.title: enveloped-data
items.text: Encrypted content plus encrypted keys for each recipient.

items.title: digested-data
items.text: Content plus a message digest of it.

items.title: encrypted-data
items.text: Encrypted content; keys are managed by other means.

items.title: authenticated-data
items.text: Content plus a MAC and recipient key information.

items.label: Key transport
items.desc: Content-encryption key encrypted in the recipient's public key. MUST support.

items.label: Key agreement
items.desc: Pairwise key from sender and recipient keys. MUST support.

items.label: Symmetric KEK
items.desc: Previously distributed key-encryption key. MUST support.

items.label: Password
items.desc: Key-encryption key derived from a password. MAY support.

items.label: Other
items.desc: Extension point for future key management techniques. MAY support.
